screens.prompt: In E3, return the salary for the ID in D3 with INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP.

hints.syntax: =INDEX(C2:C6,MATCH(D3,A2:A6,0)): the inner call produces the 3, the outer reads C4.
hints.func-index: INDEX needs the salaries in C2:C6 and a row number. On its own it has no way to know which row you want.
hints.func-match: MATCH searches A2:A6 for the ID in D3 and hands INDEX the position, which is 3.
hints.no-vlookup: VLOOKUP counts columns forward from the key, so it cannot reach a column to the left. That limit is what this exercise is about.
hints.match-exact: The third argument must be 0. Without it MATCH assumes a sorted list and never reports #N/A when an ID is missing.
hints.require-ref: Point at D3 for the ID and at the table for both ranges, so the formula still works when payroll adds a row.
hints.value: 88000 is Cy's salary, on row 4 of the sheet and third in C2:C6. Check which column INDEX reads and which one MATCH searches.
hints.error: The cell stops with #N/A because MATCH found no E-103 in A2:A6. The grader calls that an Excel error, and a stray space in the ID is the usual cause.

reject.why: MATCH is given two arguments, so the match type is missing entirely

VLOOKUP is exactly what this lesson replaces

docs.explain:
MATCH counts where a value sits inside the range you give it. E-103 sits in D3, and A2:A6 starts at E-101, so the ID lands on 3: the third cell down, which is sheet row 4. Ask MATCH on its own and 3 is all you get.

INDEX turns that count into the contents of a cell. Give it C2:C6 and the number 3, and it reads C4, where Cy's salary of 88000 sits. The answer goes in E3. The two calls are separate, so you can test the 3 before wrapping INDEX around it.

The zero in MATCH decides how it searches. Without it MATCH assumes a sorted list, so a missing ID can return a neighbouring row and the salary of the wrong person. With the zero it returns #N/A. Because each range is chosen separately, the salary column can sit left of the ID, which VLOOKUP cannot manage.

errors.text: MATCH found no exact E-103 in A2:A6, usually because the ID carries a trailing space or is stored as text.
The row number from MATCH sits past the end of C2:C6, which happens when the two ranges cover different numbers of rows.
INDEX was handed no row number, or MATCH was given the whole table where a single column belongs.

docs.atWork: Payroll and staff directories, where the column you need is chosen after the column you search.
docs.outcome: Return a value from any column, whichever side of the key it sits on.

seo.title: INDEX MATCH in Excel: look up either way
seo.description: INDEX and MATCH look up a value without column order getting in the way. MATCH finds the row, INDEX reads it, and the answer here is 88000.
